timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]

- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

text.description: For 'text': the string to type.

name.description: For 'button': hardware button to press.

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

content.content:
Exit code 1
# Why the Moonraker connection skill did not guide the two live Klipper runs (2026-11-04)

Diagnosis only; nothing edited. Runs: openai/gpt-5.4-mini via OpenRouter, build of jusprin-newui at e27c962864. Transcripts as the model saw them: `/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/cf7649d3-46dd-4047-a831-32851ae18292/scratchpad/report/{moonraker,raspberrypi}-live-chat.md`. The model's web-search results are not in the transcripts (only a "web search" marker), so what it read there is not verifiable.

## The one fact that frames everything: when the skill arrives

The skill is attached to a request only when that request carries the result of a `printer_connect` or `printer_connection_status` call (`Agent/AgentHost.cpp:3136-3139`), and only once `connection_skill()` knows the host type, which is set by the first connect attempt (`PrinterSetup/PrinterConversation.cpp:483-494`). So in both runs the model answered the opening message, added the printer, offered to connect, asked for the address and made the first connect call on the standing prompt alone. The skill's first chance to speak was the reply to "credential_requested". Verified from code and from where "[connect-moonraker skill added here]" sits in both transcripts.

The skill opens with "The rules above still apply." Where the standing prompt gives an exact sentence and the skill gives a fact that contradicts it, the exact sentence won every time (failures 1 and 6 below). The standing prompt is built in `AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`.

## Failure by failure

### 1. "Want to connect it so you can send prints straight to it?" after the person had already said so (both runs)

What the model saw: the standing prompt's connecting rule, `OFFER_AFTER_ADDING`: "after adding, offer it once: end the reply to a successful printer_add with exactly 'Want to connect it so you can send prints straight to it?' and then 'Choices: Connect it | Not now'". No condition on whether the person already asked. Both opening messages said "I want to connect it so I can send prints to it." The conduct rule "When the person plainly states what to do ... do it: call the tool without asking again" conflicts, and the literal "exactly" rule won 2 of 2. The skill was not yet in force.
Verified: the model's text matches the prompt's sentence character for character.
Kind of change: standing prompt, not skill. The offer needs an exception for a person who already asked, or the model needs leave to go straight to asking for the address.

### 2. "If you want, I can try that address now" after "can you just try it?" (run 1)

What the model saw, three texts pointing the same way:
- `printer_connect` description (`Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp:1631-1632`): "pass only hostType and the address the person gave, and until they give one, ask for it instead of calling this."
- Connecting rule: "ask for the address they open it with in a browser ... then call printer_connect".
- Conduct rule: "When you are guessing ... ask and wait for the person's answer before adding, changing or connecting one."
The 7125 address was the model's own guess, never "the address the person gave", so by those texts it had to ask first even though the person had said "just try it". The skill's "When they want to try again, call printer_connect again with the address to use" does not say whose address counts.
Inferred: consistent with every text the model had; its reasoning is not visible.
Kind of change: tool description and skill. An address the model derived and the person agreed to try is an address to use.

### 3. "Moonraker is there, but it rejected the key" when no key was typed (run 1)

What the model saw: "Connection to Voron 2.4 350 failed: The print host test failed: HTTP 401: {...}". The app's `connect()` has the credential string the form was submitted with (`PrinterConversation.cpp:826-833`) but the note never says whether it was empty. The skill says 401 is "the same answer for no key and for a wrong key" and "wants an API key, or a different one"; nothing told the model which branch it was in, and its own two previous replies had told the person to "type it there", so it assumed a key was typed. Those replies came from the standing rule "When the tool reports credential_requested, say briefly to use that form", which frames the form as something to fill; the skill's "The field can stay empty" (step 3) was in context for the first of them and did not change the wording. The form label itself says "API key (if the printer asks for one)" (`components/PrinterPanel.tsx:187`), but the model never sees the form.
Verified: the note lacks the fact. Inferred: that this is why the model picked "rejected".
Kind of change: app note after a 401 says whether a key was entered. Skill frames 401 for the common case, a person who has no key and does not know what one is.

### 4. Key URL without the port, then "the key isn't exposed that way" (run 1)

What the model saw: its search returned 

... [2115 characters truncated] ...

e premise survived.
Inferred: that no Mainsail page shows the key is from my search, not from reading Mainsail.
Kind of change: skill. State what is known instead of asking the model to find it: Mainsail and Fluidd do not show the key; the two ways to get it; and that a 401 from a printer on the same home network is most often fixed by adding this computer's network to `trusted_clients`, with no key at all. That is the labelled educated guess a stuck person needs, and the skill has nothing for it.

### 6. "It's connected now, so you can send prints straight to it" while Klipper was shut down or in error (both runs)

What the model saw: the finishing rule, "after the app says the connection is verified ... For example: It is connected, so you can send prints straight to it. You can close this chat now." Both runs reproduce the example almost verbatim. The skill's step 4 says verified "means Moonraker answered, and nothing more: it answered the same way while Klipper could not reach the printer's board", but the skill defers to the rules above it, and the app's note was just "Connection to X verified." The app has the Klipper state: `Moonraker::test` reads `klippy_state` from `/server/info` and only logs it (`src/slic3r/Utils/Moonraker.cpp:90-99`); the backend turns a pass into "verified" with no detail (`OrcaPrinterBackend.cpp:766-776`). In run 2, asked "is it ready to print right now?", the model answered correctly that it could only see that Moonraker answered, so it had understood the skill; the finishing example had already made it say the opposite.
Verified.
Kind of change: app note carries `klippy_state` (already read); finishing example stops promising sending; or the skill's fact is made a rule that outranks the example.

### 7. The "send a report" card after the second failure, although the 401 was progress (run 1)

What happened: `connection_failed()` shows the card on exactly the second failure of the chat, `++m_failed_connections != 2`, by design ("The rule is the app's, not the model's", `PrinterConversation.cpp:846-860`). It does not look at what failed. The first failure (Mainsail page) and the second (401 from Moonraker) were two different steps, the second further along.
Verified. Not a skill matter.
Kind of change: app rule. Count repeats of the same outcome, or hand the judgement to the model now that it has a skill that says which step each outcome means.

### 8. Generic Klipper kept 250 × 250 although the person said 240 × 225 (run 2)

What the model saw: in add mode the standing prompt has no word about bed size. The scope paragraph that mentions bed size ("A setting the settings tools refuse, such as its bed size, is in its printer settings on this computer") is sent only to change and connect sessions; the settings-tool rules likewise. The finding rules say "Start with just the printer model. Do not ask for nozzle, plate or filament first." The printer list gives each entry's build volume, so the model could see the mismatch, but no tool sets bed size (`printer_add` takes catalogId and nozzle only) and no rule says what to do with a stated size. Verified: the model's text matches the prompt's sentence character for character.

What the model saw, three texts pointing the same way:

# Connection skills: the lessons of 2026-11-01 to 11-03, and why the Moonraker skill still failed on 11-04

Written 2026-11-04 from the session transcripts on disk, Kenneth's own messages first. Nothing edited. Companion to `moonraker-skill-diagnosis.md` in this folder.

## The sessions where the skill was struggled over

| When | Session | What happened there |
|---|---|---|
| 10-31 to 11-01 | Printer connection agent failure (local_9758d37b) | Kenneth's P1S failed to connect; the app hid the cloud-mode printer and the model invented menus. Kenneth: "think about the nature of this problem… fix the root cause, not the symptom"; "tell me very clearly when you have moved the goalpost"; first raised letting the agent search the web. |
| 11-01 | Live Sonnet chat against the real P1S (local_8fa7e7b8 / dd354d04) | Two live chats after the tool fix went well. Kenneth: "we need a general process that can eventually result in a further improved process when more people are using it… Our current approach of doing all the heavy lifting ourselves is not practically feasible." The agent's own lesson: "producing new evidence should be the last resort"; tool results carry what is true now, a skill carries a procedure. |
| 11-01 to 11-04 | AI agent design for printer setup (local_05f541e9 / 73de5d33) | Kenneth rejected invented jargon ("one file per model", "owners fill the files") and demanded checks against OrcaSlicer's real practice; confirmed the five-point proposal: skill per connection type, added at connect time, chosen by the app; tools report observations; grows by reviewed PR plus opt-in reports; a line is written only for a state made to happen for real. |
| 11-02 | Implement the connection skill and test it on the P1S (local_4a3a2148 and its continuations a419cc62, 136dacb0, c85952ea, e4ed3f35) | The first skill was a state-to-step table; on the real P1S it told a person with the right code to re-check it. Kenneth: "The important thing is if the agent was able to guide the user throughout the process effectively and try to make educated guess… We can't just patch up for this use case. We need a mechanism that can work for most cases." Then: "The goal here is not to connect my printer." Then: "It's you wrote the wrong line… I need you to understand why you made that mistake." Then: for each failure, "lack of information? Wrong information? lack of knowledge? Wrong knowledge? What's the appropriate place to supply what's missing?" |
| 11-02 to 11-03 | Try giving the printer chat model only web_search (local_351e9202 / e0a55af0) | Four Sonnet chats on the P1S with search and no skill: the model never searched once, and stated one false fact the skill knew (a printer with LAN Only off is still heard). Recommendation: keep the skill; search alone added nothing. |
| 11-03 | Same implement session, later (1b6e3f18, ca5a0dfa, cce35003, 86306e20) | Kenneth: "add other skills for other connection types too… apply the lessons you learned from building the skill for connecting bambu." The agent listed seven lessons applied and three not applied. Kenneth caught that web search was left out of the host skills; the agent called it "a mistake, not a reasoned choice". Seven Sonnet 5.5 chats against Docker hosts all connected. Kenneth later asked why the prompt still singled out Bambu. |
| 11-02 | Fix Bambu connect tools; Tool results method (local_7d426a6b, b2d2c400) | Kenneth's test for a tool-result bug: a person stuck, told something false, right step hidden, at a cost beyond one more call. Four rules: forward the source's error; else say what the code tested; no new checks; no OrcaSlicer files. |

## The lessons, as they were stated

From Kenneth's words:

1. **Judge by the stuck person.** A skill is good if the agent guides a person who is stuck and makes labelled educated guesses. Not: whether the printer connected, whether every state is covered, whether a sentence is false.
2. **Nature of the problem, not the case.** No patch for one line; ask what stopped the model reasoning.
3. **A process that improves with use.** Verified content is not a precondition for shipping guidance; reports and PRs improve it.
4. **Search instead of guessing**, with the tool present in every chat.
5. **Classify each failure**: lack or wrong *information* (what the app knows at that moment) goes in the app's note or tool result; lack or wrong *knowledge* (how things work) goes in the skill; how to work in general goes in the prompt.
6. **Own the line you wrote** and say why you wrote it.
7. **Nothing situational in the standing prompt; a rule about one tool in its description** (older, restated in every brief).
8. **Tools report what the app saw**, forwarding the source's words.

From the agent's analysis that Kenneth approved by pressing "Yes, build it": the skill explains how the connection works; the prompt holds one way of working (likeliest guess labelled, cheapest check, drop what is ruled out, never repeat a failed step); the app reports what it observed; tests judge how the chat ends.

From the agent's 11-03 list of lessons applied to the host skills: explain, don't tabulate; write a fact only after it happened for real; app reports observations; one signal can have several causes; passing one step says nothing about the next; label guesses and state no menu paths; app picks the skill at connect time. Listed as **not applied**: tests that judge where the chat leaves the person; a real person on a real network as the test case (Docker gave "clean, induced failures").

## Were the lessons applied to the Moonraker skill? Failure by failure

| 11-04 failure | Lesson that covers it | Applied? | What I found |
|---|---|---|---|
| Redundant "Want to connect it?" | 7 (prompt holds principles) and the conduct rule "when the person plainly states what to do, do it" | **No.** The offer is an exact sentence ordered by the prompt with no exception. Kenneth's 11-03 question "do we still have Connecting is optional; after adding, offer it once…" pointed straight at this line; the answer defended the Bambu sentence next to it and nobody re-read the offer against lesson 1. Verified from `printerInstructions.ts` and the 11-03 22:14 reply. |
| "If you want, I can try that address now" | Proposal point 3: tools never carry the procedure | **Partly.** The connect tool's description still says "until they give one, ask for it instead of calling this", a procedure rule, and it outranked the person's "just try it". Verified from `ToolRegistry.cpp:1631`. |
| "It rejected the key" with no key typed | 5: lack of information goes in the app's note | **Applied to Bambu only.** The Bambu failure note got the port look; the host failure note never got "the form was submitted empty" or "with a key", although `connect()` holds the credential. The lesson was fixed into one note, not turned into a rule for every connection type's note. Verified. |
| Key URL without the port; "the key isn't exposed that way" | Explain how it works; 4 (search) | **Applied at the wrong level.** The skill explains the app's path to Moonraker (port 7125 vs the Mainsail page) and never the person's path (Moonraker's own pages, the key page included, are at Moonraker's port). Search then returned docs that omit the port, and nothing in the skill let the model apply them. The 11-03 "not applied" item, a real person on a real network, is exactly this: Docker never produced a person who had to find the key. Docs omitting the port: verified. Causal link: inferred. |
| "Mainsail's settings page", never searched | Label guesses; state no menu paths; 4 | **The guard caught the wrong thing.** The evidence test bans menu arrows and "Settings >" so the writer wrote "You have not seen where Mainsail or Fluidd show the key, so search for where their version shows it". That sentence presupposes Mainsail shows the key; my search found no such page (Mainsail's 401 FAQ points to `trusted_clients` in moonraker.conf). The guard stops stated menus but not presupposed ones. Same shape as 11-02: the writer kept the "don't be false" half of Kenneth's test and dropped the "a person stuck" half, which is recorded in memory as the 11-02 lesson and repeated here. Inferred. |
| "You can send prints straight to it" while Klipper was down | Skill step 4 says verified means only Moonraker answered; 8 (app reports what it observed) | **Applied in the skill, defeated by the prompt.** The finishing rule's worked example is that exact sentence, and the skill opens with "The rules above still apply". On 11-03 Sonnet 5.5 followed the skill ("verified only means Moonraker answered"); on 11-04 GPT-5.4 Mini followed the prompt's example. The design left a contradiction for the model to resolve, and which way it goes depends on the model. The app also reads `klippy_state` and drops it (`Moonraker.cpp:90-99`). Verified. |
| Report card after the second failure | Proposal point 4: "failed twice" | **Applied as written**, never re-examined against lesson 1. A 401 after a wrong-port failure is progress, and the count cannot tell. Verified from `PrinterConversation.cpp:849`. |
| 250 × 250 bed kept | none of the connection lessons | Add-mode prompt gap, outside the skill work. Verified. |

## Why the lessons were not enough

1. **They were proven on one model with a person who knew the answers.** The seven 11-03 chats ran Sonnet 5.5 against Docker hosts, and the scripted person had the key, took the port advice, and knew it was OctoPrint. Kenneth's test, a stuck person, was never run for a host. The two lessons the agent listed as "not applied" on 11-03 (judge where the chat leaves the person; real person on a real network) are the two the 11-04 runs failed on. Verified from the 11-03 14:00 reply and the 14:30 results table.
2. **The evidence rule shaped the skill around the app's test, not the person's situation.** "Write only what happened for real" made the skills exact about HTTP codes and silent about what a person with no key does. Docker produces every error code and no stuck person. Inferred, consistent with the guard's contents.
3. **The skill defers to a prompt nobody swept.** Three standing sentences written before any skill existed (the connect offer, "say briefly to use that form", the finishing example) give exact wording the skill's facts contradict. Lesson 7 was recited in every brief and applied to new text only, never to old. Verified.
4. **"Lack of information goes in the note" was fixed once, not made a rule.** The Bambu note got what the Bambu incident needed. No one asked, per connection type, "what does the app know at this moment that the model needs?" The host note lacks the credential state and the Klipper state. Verified.
5. **Search was treated as the fix for knowledge gaps.** The web-search-only experiment showed the model does not search unprompted, and 11-04 showed that when it does search it misapplies docs without framing. Search needs the skill to say what to look up at each stuck point and how to read the answer for this setup. Verified for the experiment; inferred for the framing.
6. **Each generalisation was done by the same agent in the same afternoon**, from one printer family to two others, with the lesson list written from memory ("You offered to help me recall lessons. If any lesson from the Bambu chats is missing above, tell me"). Nothing in the repo records how to build a connection skill; the guidance lives in two memory notes, a commit message, and a guard test. Verified: `agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md` covers skills versus tools in general and says nothing about connection skills.

## Do we have good general guidance? Not yet. What it would need to say

This is a proposal, derived from the lessons above; none of it is agreed.

1. **Start from the person's three stuck moments, not from the app's states**: what address to give; what to do when asked for a credential they do not have; what "connected" does and does not mean. For each, write the likeliest causes in order of cost to check, each labelled as app-observed, documented (with the source), or a guess. The evidence rule applies to facts about the app's own behaviour; facts about the person's side get a source label instead of being left out.

# Every time the printer chat failed to help someone connect a printer, 31 October to 4 November 2026

Short version, 4 November. Words: the **standing instructions** are what the AI reads in every printer chat. The **extra connection instructions** are added by the app the first time the person tries to connect (the code calls them "skills"); they start with "The rules above still apply", so the standing instructions win a conflict. A **message from the app** is a line the app writes into the chat for the AI, such as "Connection to X failed: HTTP 401". **LAN Only** is the Bambu setting that must be on for JusPrin to connect. The **test program** plays the person from a fixed script and cannot react.

**Run 1, 31 Oct. Kenneth's P1S, LAN Only off, the shipped app.** The app said the plug-in was installed and "the printer can be connected", with no next step, so the AI asked for an address, which is the route for other printer kinds. Asked how to find it, the AI invented menu steps, because the standing instructions demand a location for every question. The app then refused with "no printer in LAN mode is on the network" before it had listened at all, and later hid the P1S it had heard with LAN Only off. The AI repeated the same three options three times, one of them a path the chat does not have, because the standing instructions forced them.

**Run 2, 1 Nov. Same P1S, app fixed to say what it heard, Sonnet.** Outcome right. Three wrong sentences: "didn't find your P1S" seconds before it was heard, because the app's 15-second "found nothing" message read as a result and nothing said a first broadcast takes 8 to 40 s; "the search stops after 15 seconds", made from "a message after 15 seconds"; and "the printer can prepare prints", copied from the app's own words.

**Run 3, 2 Nov morning. First extra instructions, a list of one step per situation. Sonnet, slow P1S.** The line for a failure said: say the app's reason in one sentence, add no cause, tell them to compare the code. With a deliberately wrong code the AI did exactly that twice and had no new idea. With Kenneth's right code it still sent him to compare the code. The real cause, a 28-second login against a plug-in that gives up at 24, was in no message from the app, and the instructions forbade a guess. The app's word "refused" was unsupported.

**Run 4, 2 Nov evening. Rewritten instructions that explain the connection. Sonnet.** With the right code the AI reasoned well ("answered just before the attempt and then went quiet, so I can't tell whether the code was wrong"). But every failure ended in "restart the printer", because the author wrote that untested step in place of the removed one, and with a wrong code the AI never suggested checking the code. The no-printer case went from 5 of 5 to 0 of 3: the rewrite dropped "ask what the screen shows" and had nothing for the moment the app says nothing was found. The AI's notes to itself appeared in the chat. DeepSeek stated "Settings > LAN" as fact. The last two are from the author's report, not read by me.

**Run 5, 2 Nov. Web search only, no extra instructions, Sonnet, healthy P1S.** Zero searches in four chats, with nothing telling the AI to search. With no printer heard it guessed "the printer isn't in LAN mode", wrong for this app, which hears a printer either way; only the removed instructions state that. It gave the code's location as fact in one chat and as a guess in another.

**Run 6, 3 Nov. New Moonraker and OctoPrint instructions, search allowed, Sonnet, test printers in Docker, a scripted person who had the key.** Six of seven connected. The one that did not was the script ignoring a correct guess. "Nothing loaded" came from the standing instructions, which say that for any connected printer. "Mainsail's address is saved" was said before the check. The key page URL was right only because the person had typed Moonraker's port 7125; the instructions never say where Moonraker's pages live. A raw stack trace reached the person.

**Run 7, 4 Nov. Moonraker in Docker needing a key, GPT-5.4 Mini, a person who does not know what an API key is.** "Want to connect it?" after the person had asked to, ordered word for word by the standing instructions. "Please type it there" to someone with no key, from the standing instructions over the extra ones' "can stay empty". "I can try that address now" instead of trying, because the address was the AI's guess and the connect action says to use only the person's address. "It rejected the key" when none was typed, because the app's message does not say whether a key was sent. The key page URL without the port, then "the key isn't exposed that way", because Moonraker's docs omit the port and the instructions never say Moonraker's pages share its port. "Mainsail's settings page" without searching, because the instructions assume Mainsail shows the key; it does not. The report card after a failure that was progress, because the rule only counts to two. "You can send prints straight to it" with Klipper in error, because that sentence is the standing instructions' example of how to finish.

**Run 8, 4 Nov. Kenneth's Pi, no key, Klipper shut down, GPT-5.4 Mini.** The same redundant offer, the same "Mainsail's settings page", the same "send prints straight to it" (followed, when asked, by the correct "I can't see the printer's state"), and a stated 240 × 225 bed dropped without a word, since the standing instructions say nothing about bed size while adding.

### 4. Key URL without the port, then "the key isn't exposed that way" (run 1)

What the model saw: its search returned Moonraker's docs, which give `http://{moonraker-host}/access/api_key` with no port. I checked the docs: the port really is omitted there, and 7125 is Moonraker's default. The skill, in step 2 and the "Could not parse" entry, teaches that Moonraker is on 7125 and the Mainsail page is another server, but only as a matter of which address the app needs. It never says that Moonraker's own pages, the key page included, are reached at Moonraker's address and port, the same address that had just answered 401. So the model, having established "8081 is Mainsail, 7125 is Moonraker", handed the person a port-80 URL, a third server. When Chrome could not reach it, the conduct rule "When a guess is ruled out, say so and move to the next one" fit, and the model moved on instead of checking its own URL. At the same moment it called `printer_connect` a third time with nothing changed, against the rule not to repeat a failed step; my reading is that it had no next step left.
Verified: docs omit the port; the skill has no sentence about Moonraker's own pages. Inferred: the causal link.
Kind of change: skill. One sentence that the key page is at Moonraker's address and port, and that a page not reached on a different port says nothing about the key.

### 5. "Mainsail's settings page" / "an API key or access page in Mainsail's settings", never searched (both runs)

What the model saw: skill step 3, "You have not seen where Mainsail or Fluidd show the key, so search for where their version shows it before you say, and ask what they see." The sentence presupposes Mainsail shows the key somewhere. My search found no such place: Mainsail's own "connection unauthorized" FAQ sends people to `trusted_clients` in `moonraker.conf`, and Moonraker's docs give only the `/access/api_key` page and `scripts/fetch-apikey.sh`. So the model filled the skill's premise with a guess, in run 2 without any search since the one at the start of the chat, in run 1 right after two searches that had not shown such a page. The skill handed the model a sentence that says "I don't know; find out", the model found nothing, and the premise survived.
Inferred: that no Mainsail page shows the key is from my search, not from reading Mainsail.
Kind of change: skill. State what is known instead of asking the model to find it: Mainsail and Fluidd do not show the key; the two ways to get it; and that a 401 from a printer on the same home network is most often fixed by adding this computer's network to `trusted_clients`, with no key at all. That is the labelled educated guess a stuck person needs, and the skill has nothing for it.

Four rules: forward the source's error; else say what the code tested; no new checks; no OrcaSlicer files. |

## The lessons, as they were stated

From Kenneth's words:

1. **Judge by the stuck person.** A skill is good if the agent guides a person who is stuck and makes labelled educated guesses. Not: whether the printer connected, whether every state is covered, whether a sentence is false.
2. **Nature of the problem, not the case.** No patch for one line; ask what stopped the model reasoning.
3. **A process that improves with use.** Verified content is not a precondition for shipping guidance; reports and PRs improve it.
4. **Search instead of guessing**, with the tool present in every chat.
5. **Classify each failure**: lack or wrong *information* (what the app knows at that moment) goes in the app's note or tool result; lack or wrong *knowledge* (how things work) goes in the skill; how to work in general goes in the prompt.
6. **Own the line you wrote** and say why you wrote it.
7. **Nothing situational in the standing prompt; a rule about one tool in its description** (older, restated in every brief).
8. **Tools report what the app saw**, forwarding the source's words.

From the agent's analysis that Kenneth approved by pressing "Yes, build it": the skill explains how the connection works; the prompt holds one way of working (likeliest guess labelled, cheapest check, drop what is ruled out, never repeat a failed step); the app reports what it observed; tests judge how the chat ends.

From the agent's 11-03 list of lessons applied to the host skills: explain, don't tabulate; write a fact only after it happened for real; app reports observations; one signal can have several causes; passing one step says nothing about the next; label guesses and state no menu paths; app picks the skill at connect time. Listed as **not applied**: tests that judge where the chat leaves the person; a real person on a real network as the test case (Docker gave "clean, induced failures").

## Were the lessons applied to the Moonraker skill? Failure by failure

| 11-04 failure | Lesson that covers it | Applied? | What I found |
|---|---|---|---|
| Redundant "Want to connect it?" | 7 (prompt holds principles) and the conduct rule "when the person plainly states what to do, do it" | **No.** The offer is an exact sentence ordered by the prompt with no exception. Kenneth's 11-03 question "do we still have Connecting is optional; after adding, offer it once…" pointed straight at this line; the answer defended the Bambu sentence next to it and nobody re-read the offer against lesson 1. Verified from `printerInstructions.ts` and the 11-03 22:14 reply. |
| "If you want, I can try that address now" | Proposal point 3: tools never carry the procedure | **Partly.** The connect tool's description still says "until they give one, ask for it instead of calling this", a procedure rule, and it outranked the person's "just try it". Verified from `ToolRegistry.cpp:1631`. |
| "It rejected the key" with no key typed | 5: lack of information goes in the app's note | **Applied to Bambu only.** The Bambu failure note got the port look; the host failure note never got "the form was submitted empty" or "with a key", although `connect()` holds the credential. The lesson was fixed into one note, not turned into a rule for every connection type's note. Verified. |
| Key URL without the port; "the key isn't exposed that way" | Explain how it works; 4 (search) | **Applied at the wrong level.** The skill explains the app's path to Moonraker (port 7125 vs the Mainsail page) and never the person's path (Moonraker's own pages, the key page included, are at Moonraker's port). Search then returned docs that omit the port, and nothing in the skill let the model apply them. The 11-03 "not applied" item, a real person on a real network, is exactly this: Docker never produced a person who had to find the key. Docs omitting the port: verified. Causal link: inferred. |
| "Mainsail's settings page", never searched | Label guesses; state no menu paths; 4 | **The guard caught the wrong thing.** The evidence test bans menu arrows and "Settings >" so the writer wrote "You have not seen where Mainsail or Fluidd show the key, so search for where their version shows it". That sentence presupposes Mainsail shows the key; my search found no such page (Mainsail's 401 FAQ points to `trusted_clients` in moonraker.conf). The guard stops stated menus but not presupposed ones. Same shape as 11-02: the writer kept the "don't be false" half of Kenneth's test and dropped the "a person stuck" half, which is recorded in memory as the 11-02 lesson and repeated here. Inferred. |
| "You can send prints straight to it" while Klipper was down | Skill step 4 says verified means only Moonraker answered; 8 (app reports what it observed) | **Applied in the skill, defeated by the prompt.** The finishing rule's worked example is that exact sentence, and the skill opens with "The rules above still apply". On 11-03 Sonnet 5.5 followed the skill ("verified only means Moonraker answered"); on 11-04 GPT-5.4 Mini followed the prompt's example. The design left a contradiction for the model to resolve, and which way it goes depends on the model. The app also reads `klippy_state` and drops it (`Moonraker.cpp:90-99`). Verified. |
| Report card after the second failure | Proposal point 4: "failed twice" | **Applied as written**, never re-examined against lesson 1. A 401 after a wrong-port failure is progress, and the count cannot tell. Verified from `PrinterConversation.cpp:849`. |
| 250 × 250 bed kept | none of the connection lessons | Add-mode prompt gap, outside the skill work. Verified. |

## Why the lessons were not enough

1. **They were proven on one model with a person who knew the answers.** The seven 11-03 chats ran Sonnet 5.5 against Docker hosts, and the scripted person had the key, took the port advice, and knew it was OctoPrint. Kenneth's test, a stuck person, was never run for a host. The two lessons the agent listed as "not applied" on 11-03 (judge where the chat leaves the person; real person on a real network) are the two the 11-04 runs failed on. Verified from the 11-03 14:00 reply and the 14:30 results table.
2. **The evidence rule shaped the skill around the app's test, not the person's situation.** "Write only what happened for real" made the skills exact about HTTP codes and silent about what a person with no key does. Docker produces every error code and no stuck person. Inferred, consistent with the guard's contents.
3. **The skill defers to a prompt nobody swept.** Three standing sentences written before any skill existed (the connect offer, "say briefly to use that form", the finishing example) give exact wording the skill's facts contradict. Lesson 7 was recited in every brief and applied to new text only, never to old. Verified.
4. **"Lack of information goes in the note" was fixed once, not made a rule.** The Bambu note got what the Bambu incident needed. No one asked, per connection type, "what does the app know at this moment that the model needs?" The host note lacks the credential state and the Klipper state. Verified.
5. **Search was treated as the fix for knowledge gaps.** The web-search-only experiment showed the model does not search unprompted, and 11-04 showed that when it does search it misapplies docs without framing. Search needs the skill to say what to look up at each stuck point and how to read the answer for this setup. Verified for the experiment; inferred for the framing.
6. **Each generalisation was done by the same agent in the same afternoon**, from one printer family to two others, with the lesson list written from memory ("You offered to help me recall lessons. If any lesson from the Bambu chats is missing above, tell me"). Nothing in the repo records how to build a connection skill; the guidance lives in two memory notes, a commit message, and a guard test. Verified: `agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md` covers skills versus tools in general and says nothing about connection skills.

## Do we have good general guidance? Not yet. What it would need to say

This is a proposal, derived from the lessons above; none of it is agreed.

1. **Start from the person's three stuck moments, not from the app's states**: what address to give; what to do when asked for a credential they do not have; what "connected" does and does not mean. For each, write the likeliest causes in order of cost to check, each labelled as app-observed, documented (with the source), or a guess. The evidence rule applies to facts about the app's own behaviour; facts about the person's side get a source label instead of being left out.
2. **Before writing the skill, audit information against knowledge per connection type**: for each failure the app can report, list what it knows at that moment (was the credential empty, what did Klipper say, which port answered) and put it in the note. The skill is written to the notes that exist.
3. **Sweep the standing prompt and the tool descriptions** for any exact sentence or step about connecting, and delete it or make it conditional, because a skill cannot override "exactly".
4. **Test with Kenneth's test**: a scripted person who does not have the answer (no key, wrong port, Klipper down, `.local` name that fails), on the weakest model the product ships by default, judged by where the person ends up. A run where the person knows everything proves nothing about guidance.
5. **Tell the model what to search for and how to apply it** at each stuck point, since it does not search on its own and misreads docs for this setup.
6. **Decide when the skill arrives.** Today it comes after the first connect call, so anything the person needs before that (the address and port for a Klipper printer) is the prompt's job or the skill's trigger must move earlier.

Sources for the two web checks in the companion note: Mainsail FAQ "connection unauthorized", Moonraker authorization and installation docs.

# Every time the printer chat failed to help someone connect a printer, 31 October to 4 November 2026

Short version, 4 November. Words: the **standing instructions** are what the AI reads in every printer chat. The **extra connection instructions** are added by the app the first time the person tries to connect (the code calls them "skills"); they start with "The rules above still apply", so the standing instructions win a conflict. A **message from the app** is a line the app writes into the chat for the AI, such as "Connection to X failed: HTTP 401". **LAN Only** is the Bambu setting that must be on for JusPrin to connect. The **test program** plays the person from a fixed script and cannot react.

**Run 1, 31 Oct. Kenneth's P1S, LAN Only off, the shipped app.** The app said the plug-in was installed and "the printer can be connected", with no next step, so the AI asked for an address, which is the route for other printer kinds. Asked how to find it, the AI invented menu steps, because the standing instructions demand a location for every question. The app then refused with "no printer in LAN mode is on the network" before it had listened at all, and later hid the P1S it had heard with LAN Only off. The AI repeated the same three options three times, one of them a path the chat does not have, because the standing instructions forced them.

**Run 2, 1 Nov. Same P1S, app fixed to say what it heard, Sonnet.** Outcome right. Three wrong sentences: "didn't find your P1S" seconds before it was heard, because the app's 15-second "found nothing" message read as a result and nothing said a first broadcast takes 8 to 40 s; "the search stops after 15 seconds", made from "a message after 15 seconds"; and "the printer can prepare prints", copied from the app's own words.

**Run 3, 2 Nov morning. First extra instructions, a list of one step per situation. Sonnet, slow P1S.** The line for a failure said: say the app's reason in one sentence, add no cause, tell them to compare the code. With a deliberately wrong code the AI did exactly that twice and had no new idea. With Kenneth's right code it still sent him to compare the code. The real cause, a 28-second login against a plug-in that gives up at 24, was in no message from the app, and the instructions forbade a guess. The app's word "refused" was unsupported.

**Run 4, 2 Nov evening. Rewritten instructions that explain the connection. Sonnet.** With the right code the AI reasoned well ("answered just before the attempt and then went quiet, so I can't tell whether the code was wrong"). But every failure ended in "restart the printer", because the author wrote that untested step in place of the removed one, and with a wrong code the AI never suggested checking the code. The no-printer case went from 5 of 5 to 0 of 3: the rewrite dropped "ask what the screen shows" and had nothing for the moment the app says nothing was found. The AI's notes to itself appeared in the chat. DeepSeek stated "Settings > LAN" as fact. The last two are from the author's report, not read by me.

**Run 5, 2 Nov. Web search only, no extra instructions, Sonnet, healthy P1S.** Zero searches in four chats, with nothing telling the AI to search. With no printer heard it guessed "the printer isn't in LAN mode", wrong for this app, which hears a printer either way; only the removed instructions state that. It gave the code's location as fact in one chat and as a guess in another.

**Run 6, 3 Nov. New Moonraker and OctoPrint instructions, search allowed, Sonnet, test printers in Docker, a scripted person who had the key.** Six of seven connected. The one that did not was the script ignoring a correct guess. "Nothing loaded" came from the standing instructions, which say that for any connected printer. "Mainsail's address is saved" was said before the check. The key page URL was right only because the person had typed Moonraker's port 7125; the instructions never say where Moonraker's pages live. A raw stack trace reached the person.

**Run 7, 4 Nov. Moonraker in Docker needing a key, GPT-5.4 Mini, a person who does not know what an API key is.** "Want to connect it?" after the person had asked to, ordered word for word by the standing instructions. "Please type it there" to someone with no key, from the standing instructions over the extra ones' "can stay empty". "I can try that address now" instead of trying, because the address was the AI's guess and the connect action says to use only the person's address. "It rejected the key" when none was typed, because the app's message does not say whether a key was sent. The key page URL without the port, then "the key isn't exposed that way", because Moonraker's docs omit the port and the instructions never say Moonraker's pages share its port. "Mainsail's settings page" without searching, because the instructions assume Mainsail shows the key; it does not. The report card after a failure that was progress, because the rule only counts to two. "You can send prints straight to it" with Klipper in error, because that sentence is the standing instructions' example of how to finish.

**Run 8, 4 Nov. Kenneth's Pi, no key, Klipper shut down, GPT-5.4 Mini.** The same redundant offer, the same "Mainsail's settings page", the same "send prints straight to it" (followed, when asked, by the correct "I can't see the printer's state"), and a stated 240 × 225 bed dropped without a word, since the standing instructions say nothing about bed size while adding.
